node.label: Jane Burbank
node.date_label: Intelligentsia and Revolution (1986) · Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004) · Empires in World History, with Frederick Cooper (2010)
node.description: In Empires in World History (2010), written with Frederick Cooper, Jane Burbank argues that empires governed through differences among populations and changing repertoires of power. Their comparison treats the nation-state as a contingent political arrangement rather than history’s necessary destination. Bronwen Everill praises the comparative case studies but criticizes the unclear distinction between empire and nation-state and the limited treatment of empires outside Eurasia. Burbank’s Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004) challenges the image of peasants as outsiders to law, showing rural people using courts to settle disputes through formal legal procedures. Alexandra Oberländer credits this revision of peasant stereotypes while criticizing the predominance of statistical evidence and questioning the framing in terms of civil society. Burbank’s studies connect everyday legal practice with the institutions and political possibilities of empire.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Intelligentsia and Revolution (1986); Imperial Russia: New Histories for the Empire (coedited with David L. Ransel, 1998); “Insult and Punishment in Rural Courts” (1999); Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004); Russian Empire: Space, People, Power, 1700–1930 (coedited with Mark von Hagen and Anatolyi Remnev, 2007); Empires in World History (with Frederick Cooper, 2010); Post-Imperial Possibilities (with Frederick Cooper, 2023).
node.scope_note: Selected primary pages 147–150 and 165–167 of the 1999 rural-courts article and the complete published interview (173–180) read. Book arguments otherwise mediated through named reviews and publisher descriptions; complete monographs unread. Benton acknowledgment read directly at xiv. The 2006 rights-regime article and 2013 chapter remain unread beyond available metadata or abstract. No full reading of the 2007 introduction claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burbank and Cooper coauthored Empires in World History (2010), comparing imperial strategies for ruling diverse populations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: JSTOR authorship/copyright and book description; NYU bibliography corroborates. Coauthorship only: joint argument retained, full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Search for Sovereignty (2010), Benton credits Burbank and Cooper jointly with sharing ideas about imperial political imagination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher front matter, printed xiv, paragraph beginning The NYU History Department: “generously shared their ideas” about “imperial political imagination.” Specific intellectual exchange; no sole origin or full-book debt asserted. Later chapters unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Tony Ballantyne’s 2014 review reads Burbank and Cooper’s Empires in World History (2010) as confirming Bayly’s Imperial Meridian on the connection between weakening Muslim empires and European maritime ascendancy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Empires in History section, paragraph beginning The growing ability of Europeans, and note 10: “confirm the outlines.” Reader-mediated agreement, not demonstrated influence or personal contact. Both monographs unread in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: Empires in World History (2010), coauthored with Cooper, explains political possibilities through comparisons and interactions among empires rather than an inevitable transition to nation-states.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Everill review, opening, chapter-one discussion and concluding evaluation: “repertoires of power.” Her limited-Eurasian-coverage criticism remains explicit; full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the interview Paysans et intellectuels en Russie (1999), Burbank proposes studying rural people’s changing experiences instead of assuming an isolated, timeless peasantry.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Burbank’s answers, pp. 173–176: “individualize the experience” (174). Contribution to social-history questions, not membership in a unified school. Complete interview read; cited studies unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Insult and Punishment in Rural Courts (1999), Burbank argues that rural litigation connected villagers to state authority and helped produce a civic ideal.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary pp. 165–166, especially final paragraph: “a civic ideal.” Institutional participation is not equated with loyalty to autocracy; middle case analyses unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Russian Peasants Go to Court (2004) combines close reading of cases with statistical evidence to reconstruct rural legal practice, as Gregory L. Freeze’s review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Freeze, displayed extract, first paragraph, p. 1284: “statistical data set.” A methodological contribution, not a claim of cliometric affiliation; full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Jane Burbank and Frederick Cooper's Empires in World History (2010) contributes to nationalism studies by challenging the inevitability of the nation-state, an argument Eric T. Jennings takes up in ‘The French Empire’ (2023) to reconsider how nations and empires developed together.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's displayed Summary and Further Reading, not the restricted chapter body. The Summary explicitly names both authors, explains their challenge to national inevitability, and uses it to frame the chapter's investigation of French imperial nationalism and federal alternatives. This supports a bounded contribution to nationalism studies; the mapping to that existing field node is editorial. Jennings has no endpoint in the supplied lists, so no personal edge is proposed. Cooper retains equal credit. Everill's complete review was also read and independently confirms the book's challenge to an automatic empire-to-nation transition, while criticizing its conceptual distinction between those forms.

proposed_edges.relationship: Jane Burbank and Frederick Cooper's Post-Imperial Possibilities: Eurasia, Eurafrica, Afroasia (2023) contributes to intellectual history by examining Eurasia, Eurafrica and Afroasia as political projects for reorganizing the world beyond existing empires and nation-states.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Puri's displayed publisher Extract only, not the full review or book. It explains each of the three projects and expressly distinguishes the history of ideas from their partial practical realization. Also read Sergey Glebov's displayed AHR review Extract, which describes alternatives beyond national sovereignty and identifies the original Princeton publication as 2023. Puri reviews a 2024 edition; the relationship retains the original year. The field classification is an editorial mapping of the explicitly described intellectual projects, not a claim that either reviewer uses the precise field label. Both coauthors are credited; neither reviewer has a supplied endpoint.
